profile.address: 3400 Horizon Drive, King of Prussia, PA 19406
profile.reading:
DaStor operates a boutique enterprise colocation and data center facility at 3400 Horizon Drive in King of Prussia, Pennsylvania, a large mixed use office and business park roughly twenty miles northwest of Philadelphia along the Pennsylvania Turnpike and Route 202 corridor. According to the company's own published specifications, the building totals 22,000 square feet and offers 4 megawatts of power, backed by N plus 1 generator redundancy, a 2N uninterruptible power supply configuration, N plus 1 cooling, and dual, 2N network paths for connectivity. The site is described as having controlled access security and surveillance along with direct access to major fiber routes running through the King of Prussia business corridor, a location long favored by telecommunications and IT companies for its proximity to Philadelphia, its highway access, and its dense fiber infrastructure.

This King of Prussia address also serves as DaStor's corporate headquarters. The company was founded by Kevin Mulqueen, who serves as chief executive and brings close to three decades of telecommunications and data center industry experience to the business. Before starting DaStor, Mulqueen led colocation operations at Crown Castle Fiber, where he oversaw a portfolio of more than twenty facilities generating roughly 48 million dollars in annual revenue, and earlier founded Cross Connect Solutions, a carrier neutral colocation company that was later acquired by Sidera Networks. He also spent thirteen years in senior sales roles at ATX Telecommunications before moving into data center operations. DaStor positions itself as a smaller, relationship driven alternative to the large wholesale and hyperscale colocation providers, emphasizing transparent, published pricing without long negotiated contracts, and direct access to engineers rather than a tiered customer service model.

Beyond King of Prussia, the company operates additional enterprise grade facilities across the greater Philadelphia metropolitan region, offering colocation, cloud, storage, backup, disaster recovery, and network services aimed at mid market and enterprise customers who want dedicated support without the scale and complexity of a large multi tenant campus. The company does not publish independently verified certifications such as an SSAE 18 audit or an Uptime Institute Tier rating for this specific building, nor does it disclose current tenancy, so those details remain outside the public record for now.

reading.body:
DāStor's King of Prussia facility is a 22,000 square foot enterprise colocation campus with 4 megawatts of published power capacity. At 40 kW per rack, a common density for enterprise and cloud workloads, this translates to roughly 100 racks under full IT load. The site sits in Pennsylvania's King of Prussia business corridor, a mature telecom hub northwest of Philadelphia with direct access to major fiber routes, and ranks fourth among the four facilities in Pennsylvania with published power specifications, accounting for 18 percent of the state's 22.2 megawatts of announced capacity.

The campus qualifies as N plus 1 redundant on generators and cooling, with 2N UPS and dual 2N network paths. The site publishes no independent certifications such as SSAE 18 audit or Uptime Institute Tier rating, and current tenancy is not disclosed. DāStor operates the facility as part of a regional portfolio of smaller enterprise-grade sites across greater Philadelphia, positioning itself as relationship-driven colocation for mid-market and enterprise customers rather than hyperscale wholesale.

For AI workloads, this campus does not approach the density or scale required for training. At 4 megawatts, it is roughly 250 times smaller than the gigawatt-scale campuses now competing to host frontier model training. The enterprise-focused architecture, the published lack of specialized certifications, and the regional rather than national footprint all indicate this site serves traditional colocation customers, not the accelerator-dense infrastructure pools that drive AI scaling.
